keep.why: Adds a caveat: even in a recharge oscillator model, timing of strong El Niños can be unpredictable despite heat accumulation.
This paper finds a mechanism that can make strong El Niño events unpredictable, supporting the dashboard's caveat that past events are no guide here.
This early warning study forecasts a moderate-to-strong El Niño for 2023 with an 89 percent onset chance, adding an independent forecast to the event assessment.
Explains how a temperature difference across the equatorial Pacific can distinguish the eastern Pacific type of El Niño from the central Pacific type.
Shows how the 2017 El Niño's heavy rains and floods disrupted spending in Peru, illustrating economic harm on South America's coast.
Cautions that the strength of extreme events like those in 1982 and 1997 can switch unpredictably, limiting forecasts of harsh impacts.
Forecast before 2023 that El Niño would add about 0.2°C and likely make 2024 the hottest year on record.
Shows 2023's global warmth was also driven by record-low albedo, a caveat to attributing all warming to El Niño.
It shows how the ocean and atmosphere exchange energy, which creates El Niño's global weather signature.
It links large scale air temperature patterns to El Niño phases, showing how atmospheric coupling shapes the event.
It measures how the 2017 El Niño changed consumer spending in Peru, showing economic impacts far from the warm water.
Explains that El Nino raises global temperature by about +0.2C and likely made 2024 the hottest year.
Adds caveat that 2023's warming surge was also driven by record-low sunlight reflection, not just El Nino.
Finds sea surface temperatures rose in sharp persistent steps in 1925/26 and 1987/88 rather than smooth or temporary spikes.
Measures tropical Atlantic sea surface temperature indices and finds strong persistence, supporting a stayed shift rather than a spike.
Explains that record-low planetary albedo from fewer low clouds amplified the recent global temperature surge beyond known drivers.
Uses global temperature data to show an El Nino spike can top the record without starting a new lasting level.
Finds tropical Atlantic sea surface temperature indices are strongly persistent, so rises tend to stay rather than reverse.
Shows in a conceptual model that climate components can cross thresholds and settle into new stable states.
It shows models missed a record low cloud cover that amplified the 2023 heat, so forecasts can lag reality and need upward revisions.
It reports an early warning method that predicted the 2023 El Nino onset and strength, so model forecast shifts can be meaningful.
It explains that scarce observations and climate model biases limit El Niño forecasts, and a hybrid model improves skill.
It shows standard El Niño forecasts lose skill after six months and that machine learning can improve that skill.
It shows that scarce data makes learning El Niño variability hard, but pre-training on climate models helps.
Explains how a warmer upper ocean and stronger layering can strengthen El Nino, so a record hot ocean may mean forecasts see a different system.
It cautions that record-low planetary albedo amplified the 2023 global temperature surge, so other factors can shift the peak warmth.
Bank card data from Peru show El Nino shifted consumer spending and marked a recovery time, matching delayed economic impacts.
Explains that El Nino adds about 0.2 degrees Celsius to global air temperature, so the hottest year comes after onset.
Caveat: low cloud cover also helped cause the 2023 heat spike, so ocean heat is not the only driver.
Finds 2023 warming beat model estimates by 0.2 K and links the gap to record low planetary albedo.
Shows global radiative feedback weakened recently, making observed warming stronger than many models assume.
Shows CFSv2 made a correct monsoon forecast for the wrong physical reason, so a model can score well yet still be biased.
Reports a network model outperforming CFSv2 and SEAS5, supporting that existing seasonal forecast systems can underperform.
It gives a separate 2026 ENSO forecast that also expected neutral or a weak event, illustrating forecasts undershot the observed ONI.
Model biases in the West African monsoon and its ENSO teleconnection help explain the weak mixed rainfall signal.
Shows early winter El Nino can nudge the North Atlantic Oscillation positive and late winter negative, while models struggle with this link.
Shows that El Niño weakens Sahel summer rainfall mainly by cutting heavy daily rain events, the main source of year-to-year variability.
Finds in Sahel croplands that El Niño tends to reduce harvest-time political violence while La Niña increases it, adding nuance to conflict risk.
Maps Iran's seasonal precipitation response to ENSO, PDO and NAO, showing winter is most affected.
Assesses El Niño effects on warm and cold winters in northern Eurasia, supporting the mild European Russia tendency and its limits.
Measures how Eastern Pacific El Niño raises the odds of very dry western and wet central Pacific seasons.
Explains that El Niño type (east or central Pacific warming) switches which Pacific islands get dry or wet.
Links Paraná streamflow variability to solar cycles and El Niño, which can help explain flood risk in the basin.
Develops a method to estimate the baseline averages used for Niño 3.4 temperature anomalies, relevant under climate change.
Forecasts El Niño onset and magnitude from temperature anomaly patterns inside Niño 3.4, showing its predictive value.
Shows eastern Pacific El Niño events bring very high or low seasonal rain over wider areas than central Pacific events, matching stronger coastal impacts.
Uses card transaction data from the 2017 El Niño in Peru to measure how floods changed spending and which merchants were affected.
Measures where El Niño and La Niña make regions warmer or cooler, supporting mirrored weather effects.
Finds La Niña phases raise weather-related power outages in the US, showing its weather impacts.
Shows strong El Nino events can be unpredictably strong, though they peak in northern winter and affect global weather.
Explains how links between air temperature patterns make El Nino grow and then decay after northern winter, so events last about a year.
Measures how El Nino breaks many links in a global climate network, supporting the claim that it changes weather on half the planet.
Explains that zonal sea surface temperature differences in the tropical Pacific can indicate whether an El Niño is central or eastern Pacific type.
It shows standard 30-year normals for Niño 3.4 can be biased under warming, so ONI anomalies may need adjusted baselines.
Shows eastern Pacific events produce broader precipitation anomalies than central Pacific events, so their impacts differ.
Shows eastern and central Pacific El Niño types can be separated early and that their regional rainfall impacts differ.
Explains climate normals as multi-decade averages and anomalies as departures from them, the same concept used for 1991-2020.
Proposes a real-time filter for climate normals and anomalies that accounts for warming trends, improving above-trend anomaly estimates.
Shows the long SOI record contains enough signal to predict ENSO years ahead, supporting its use as an atmospheric ENSO index.
Demonstrates a nonanticipative analog method for forecasting temperature extremes from past observations, no climate model.
Deep learning for extreme events often lacks enough historical data, so it adds physics and simulated data to cope.
A hybrid ML-physics model reproduces ENSO teleconnections but shows deficiencies in nonlinear response and under out-of-distribution warming.
Shows ENSO forecast skill normally falls beyond six months, the basis for treating lead 6 errors as expected.
Measures ENSO phase skill out to 22-24 months, showing lead 6 is not a hard limit for all models.
Shows subsurface heat leads surface warming, supporting the fuel gauge idea.
Explains how climate normals and anomalies are estimated, and warns standard baselines can be biased in a changing climate.
Shows seasonal forecast models capture the ENSO to Atlantic hurricane link but overstate it, meaning it is statistical not deterministic.
Finds El Nino phases produce episodic breakdowns and strong teleconnections, supporting the usual not guaranteed framing.
Links recurring mid latitude circulation patterns to teleconnections, showing the atmospheric rearrangement behind remote links.
Shows climate change has shifted teleconnection patterns, so these statistical links are not fixed.
Shows how equatorial wind stress shifts the ocean's warm layer, supporting the idea that trades are an engine of ENSO.
Explains how seasonal baselines for Niño 3.4 are estimated and warns that standard 30-year normals can be biased under climate change.
It finds a running total of El Nino and La Nina explains about half of tropospheric temperature variation, matching delayed ocean heating.
Shows El Nino shocks during the crop growing season change harvest related conflict only in exposed croplands, so impacts are local and seasonal.
Maps how different El Nino types bring very low or high seasonal rainfall to particular regions, shaping agricultural production there.
Finds El Nino temperature links are concentrated in limited areas and much of the globe is unaffected, so impacts are localized.
Models the ocean atmosphere coupling that gives ENSO its global climate signature and distant impacts.
Questions the standard SOI pressure index and suggests sea surface temperature differences capture atmospheric response better.
Shows a machine learning model reproduces coupled ocean atmosphere dynamics including El Nino, supporting the link.
Explains that standard deterministic SST reconstructions like ERSST may understate observation uncertainty; offers a probabilistic alternative.
In model projections, subsurface warming is linked to later surface warming, supporting the idea that El Nino heat builds below first.
Radiosonde profiles over Italy show temperature oscillations change phase with height and vary by layer, backing the whole air column view.
Models westerly wind bursts as noise that amplifies El Niño, with stronger events having more bursts.
Proposes a real time filter for wind anomalies, useful background for the two sigma threshold.
Finds record low planetary albedo from fewer low clouds boosted absorbed sunlight, helping explain the recent jump in Earth's energy imbalance.
Shows how El Nino wind patterns can create the sea surface temperature pattern of an Indian Ocean Dipole.
Quantifies how El Nino controls the Indian Ocean Dipole, mainly at its peak.
Finds the Indian Ocean Dipole influence on Indian rainfall becomes clearer once El Nino is removed.
Models how MJO wind forcing can trigger ENSO events, supporting the idea that the MJO times the pushes.
Uses a stochastic model to capture interactions between wind, MJO and ENSO, adding evidence for the coupling.
Quantifies how MEI links multiple tropical Pacific variables and tracks coupled variability.
Measures how ENSO crop-growing-season shocks change postharvest conflict in exposed croplands, strongest in Southern Africa and the Sahel.
Shows EP and CP El Niños leave different footprints in extreme seasonal rainfall, with EP affecting larger areas.
Finds the east-west Pacific temperature contrast signals whether an upcoming El Niño will be Eastern or Central Pacific.
Shows how Central and Eastern Pacific El Niño patterns can arise from combined intraseasonal, interannual and decadal processes.
Uses a simple El Niño model to show weak forcing can cause irregular switching that limits strong event predictability.
Finds an intrinsic predictability limit for strong El Niño events from irregular switching between oscillatory and chaotic states.
Shows model skill is limited by missing ENSO nonlinearity, and a nonlinear model from observations improves prediction and reduces the spring predictability barrier.
Notes climate model biases and linear models missing warm-cold asymmetry, and a hybrid model capturing that asymmetry improves ENSO forecasts.
